title: Love those who stumble
hook: love even those who do wrong; they're kin and err unwillingly (Meditations 7.22)

segments.voice: Yesterday: all will forget, the two forgettings that loosen reputation's grip. Your line was all will forget. Did you do one honest thing anyway? Day five hundred ninety.

A toddler learning to walk falls over. Nobody gets angry at the toddler. Nobody says, he's doing that to me. We see a small person who hasn't learned yet, and we reach out a hand. Now picture an adult who lies to you, or snaps at you, or lets you down. The reaching hand disappears. Marcus Aurelius wondered whether the two cases are as different as they feel. In book seven he says something that sounds almost impossible.
screen: `A TODDLER FALLS.` → `NOBODY GETS ANGRY.` → `AN ADULT FALLS.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Meditations seven, twenty-two, opens, in George Long's translation: "It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong." Peculiar here means distinctive, belonging to us. Marcus thinks this is what makes a human being human. Animals can love those who are good to them. People can love those who aren't. Second, how. Marcus doesn't just command it. He gives four reasons that make it possible. Remember that they're your kin, part of the same human family. Remember that they do wrong through ignorance, without meaning to, the way Socrates taught that nobody does wrong willingly. Remember that very soon both of you will be dead. And above all, remember that they haven't actually harmed you, because they haven't made your own mind any worse. Third, the hard part. The second reason is the one people argue with. Doesn't some harm look deliberate? Marcus would say: they chose it because they misjudged what was good, like someone stumbling in the dark. That's why today's title says stumble. It doesn't excuse the wrong. It changes how you hold the person. Fourth, what it isn't. Loving someone who stumbles doesn't mean pretending they didn't, or letting them keep doing it. Marcus judged cases and ran an empire. He corrected people. But he tried to correct them the way you'd steady a toddler: firmly, without hatred, and wishing them well.
screen: `TO LOVE EVEN WRONGDOERS.` · `KIN, IGNORANT, MORTAL, HARMLESS.` · `STUMBLING IN THE DARK.` · `CORRECT WITHOUT HATRED.` · then, large: `KIN WHO STUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind someone who did you wrong, not the worst thing, just a real one. Picture them. Now try Marcus's four thoughts, slowly. They're kin. They stumbled, misjudging what was good. We'll both be gone soon. They haven't touched who I am. If you can, wish them well, quietly, in your own words. If you can't today, just sit with the trying. The bell holds the time.
Love those who stumble. Marcus's claim that loving even wrongdoers is distinctly human, because they're kin who err without meaning to. Today's word.
Your line: kin who stumble. Today, wish one wrongdoer well, silently, even as you keep your boundaries. Day five hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes rehearse the four thoughts of 7.22 (kinship, ignorance, mortality, no real harm) when they've been wronged, as a way to wish the person well while still correcting or avoiding the wrong.

fork.setup: someone lied to you, and you're furious. which thought does Marcus give himself first?
fork.reveal: Meditations 7.22: remember they're kin, they do wrong through ignorance, you'll both soon die, and they haven't harmed your mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: love your enemies means pretending they're good.
what it means: see wrongdoers as kin who stumbled, wish them well, and still deal honestly with the wrong.
what a scholar hears: 7.22 rests on the Socratic idea that no one errs willingly, which the Stoics adopted: wrongdoing is a mistaken judgment about the good.

sources.quoted: It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong.

notes: Confirm Long's wording of the opening of 7.22.
The four reasons in 7.22 (kinship, ignorance and unwillingness, both soon dead, no harm to the ruling faculty) are paraphrased; confirm.
The Socratic 'no one errs willingly' reference (Protagoras 345d–e) should be checked.
The word 'stumble' is the path's title, not Marcus's term.
